subject: Biology
title: Grasslands and Savannas
description: A quick, practical guide to Grasslands and Savannas.

hook.text: Grasslands cover a quarter of Earth's land surface. They're too dry for forests, too wet for deserts.

buildup.text: African savannas host the greatest wildlife spectacles—millions of wildebeest migrate each year.

discovery.text: Grass survives grazing because it grows from the base, not the tip. Mow it and it bounces back.

twist.text: Much of the world's grassland has been converted to farmland. It's the most transformed biome.

climax.text: Grassland soils store enormous amounts of carbon in deep root systems—more stable than forest carbon.

punchline.text: Grass looks simple. It's anything but.

quiz.question: How does grass survive being grazed or mowed?
options: It grows from the base, not the tip
It regrows from seeds each time

details.summary: Grasslands and savannas are ecosystems dominated by grasses with few or scattered trees, covering about 40 percent of Earth's land surface. Fire, grazing, and seasonal drought maintain these ecosystems by preventing tree encroachment and recycling nutrients.
details.whyItMatters: Grasslands support vast populations of grazing animals and store enormous amounts of carbon in their deep roots and soils. Conversion to cropland has destroyed most temperate grasslands, making them among the most endangered ecosystems.
takeaways: Fire and grazing prevent grasslands from transitioning to forest
Grassland soils store more carbon than the vegetation above them
Temperate grasslands are among Earth's most converted and endangered biomes

faq.question: Why are grasslands important for carbon storage?
faq.answer: Grassland plants invest heavily in root systems that can extend meters deep. When roots die, they deposit carbon in soil where it can remain stable for centuries. This belowground carbon storage is more resistant to fire than forest carbon stored in trees.

faq.question: What is the difference between a grassland and a savanna?
faq.answer: Grasslands have continuous grass cover with virtually no trees. Savannas have scattered trees over a grass understory, typically in tropical regions with distinct wet and dry seasons. The African savanna is the classic example with its iconic scattered acacia trees.
